new_statements.quote: Contrary to previous claims (e.g. Jones 1986c; Donohue 2004), I argue there is no word-level stress in Yawa-Saweru. Instead, prosodic patterns operate at the level of the intonational phrase. ... The IP is also defined by a single Prosodically Most Prominent Syllable (PMPS). ... In Saweru, this PMPS is characterized by increased duration and a pitch peak. [p.95:] The main marker for the finality status of a phrase in Saweru is the position of the PMPS. For phrases of the final type, the penultimate syllable is the PMPS, whereas for phrases of the non-final type, the ultimate syllable is the PMPS. The primary characteristic of a Saweru PMPS is increased duration.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Saweru has no lexical/word-level stress (explicitly rejecting Donohue 2004's lexical-foot analysis). Prominence is assigned once per intonational phrase: the single most prominent syllable is the PENULT of a sentence-final (independent) phrase, with devoicing and final-consonant deletion of the following ultima, and the FINAL syllable of a non-final (dependent) phrase with rising pitch; the PMPS is marked chiefly by at least doubled duration, secondarily by the phrasal pitch peak, intensity being an unreliable by-product. A word in isolation/declarative citation is a final phrase, so citation forms surface with penultimate prominence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None at word level; longer phrases may show additional 'intermediate phrase' high-low pitch waves before the final boundary tone (fn.14, p.97), not analysed as secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Nasal codas /m n/ are devoiced rather than deleted in the post-PMPS ultima; intensity on the PMPS is optional (fn.13); corpus is narrative-heavy so other phrase types may exist (fn.12). Earlier analyses (Donohue 2004: lexically determined binary/ternary feet with variable stress position; Donohue n.d. marks stress with acute accents) treat Saweru as having lexical stress -- van Schie attributes those patterns to phrase position.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the Intonational Phrase, not the word; final-phrase (incl. single-word declaratives/citation) = penultimate PMPS, non-final phrase = ultimate PMPS. Based on first-hand fieldwork on Saweru Island (19 h, 6 speakers) with acoustic measurements (non-PMPS syllables ~150 ms, PMPS 300-400 ms).
new_statements.identity_note: van Schie 2026 describes Saweru proper (sawe1240; speakers born and raised on Saweru Island, her own 2020s fieldwork corpus 'van Schie 2025a'), treated as one of three Yawa-Saweru varieties alongside Ambaidiru and Turu (both Yawa, nucl1454). The headline claim 'no word-level stress in Yawa-Saweru' is family-wide, but sec. 3.6.2 gives the Saweru-specific facts (penultimate PMPS in final phrases, ultimate in non-final, duration-cued). Note the source conflict: Donohue 2004 (unseen, unpublished) analyses the same language as having lexically determined stress/foot structure; the catalog entry should flag 'no word stress per van Schie 2026, contra Donohue 2004 lexical'. Crossref gives Donohue 2001 pages as 291-306, not Glottolog's 321-336.

sources.note: Summarises Donohue (2004) second-hand: for Saweru Donohue 'constructs a complicated set of rules of binary and ternary feet with initial, penultimate and antepenultimate stress within the foot' and 'concludes that both foot length and the position of stress are lexically determined' (Donohue 2004:10 quoted as calling an alternative 'no less arbitrary than the model proposed'); van Schie proposes instead no lexical stress, a phrasal system with one most prominent syllable per intonational phrase.
